title: Camillae infantia. Pugna equestris
titleEn: Camilla's Childhood and the Cavalry Battle — Aeneid XI.532–647
source: P. Vergilius Maro, Aeneid, ed. J. B. Greenough, The Bucolics, Aeneid, and Georgics of Virgil (Boston: Ginn & Company, 1881), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0690.phi003.perseus-lat2, sha256 e639e6a0e27427ef. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Greenough's spelling kept (volnus, divom, Karthago, -is accusatives); his quotation marks printed as “ ”. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: While Turnus lies in wait in the hills, the poem turns to heaven. Diana, daughter of Latona, speaks sadly to Opis, one of her nymphs: Camilla is riding to a war that will kill her, and the goddess's love for her is old. Then comes Camilla's story. Metabus, king of the Volscian town of Privernum, was driven out for his harsh rule and fled with his baby daughter, whom he named Camilla after her mother Casmilla. Cornered by pursuers at the flooded river Amasenus, he bound the child to his spear, vowed her to Diana as her servant, and hurled her across; then he swam over and took her up. No city would shelter him, and he raised her in the wild mountains on mares' milk, armed her as soon as she could walk, and dressed her in a tiger's skin; she hunted cranes and swans with sling and javelin, and turned away every offer of marriage to serve Diana. The goddess wishes she had kept out of this war, and since her fate is fixed she sends Opis down with an arrow of vengeance for whoever wounds her, promising to carry the body home in a cloud. Then the cavalry battle begins: the Trojans and Etruscans advance on the city, Messapus, Coras and Camilla's squadron ride out against them, and the spears fly like snow. Aconteus is killed in the first shock, the Latins break for the walls, rally, and are driven back again, the two sides surging to and fro like the tide on a beach; at the third clash the lines lock together, Orsilochus brings down Remulus by wounding his horse, and Catillus kills Iollas and the giant Herminius.
part: Camilla's Childhood and the Cavalry Battle (XI.532–647)

sentences.t:
Velocem interea superis in sedibus Opim,
unam ex virginibus sociis sacraque caterva,
compellabat et has tristis Latonia voces
ore dabat:
sentences.l:
Swift, meanwhile, in the seats above, Opis,
one of the maidens her companions and her sacred band,
was addressing, and these sad words Latona's daughter
from her mouth was giving:
sentences.i: Meanwhile, in the dwellings on high, the daughter of Latona was speaking to swift Opis, one of the maidens who were her companions in her holy band, and these were the sorrowful words she uttered:
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough: the scene moves from Turnus's ambush to heaven. 'Opim', accusative of 'Opis', in '-im' as Latin often gives Greek names in '-is', a nymph of Diana's company. 'unam ex virginibus sociis sacraque caterva', 'one of her companion maidens and holy band'. 'Latonia', 'Latona's daughter', Diana, the twin of Apollo. 'compellabat… dabat', imperfects that set the scene, 'interea', while Turnus lies in wait. 'tristis… voces', '-is' accusative plural, 'sad words' ('tristis' could also be nominative, 'the sorrowing goddess'); 'ore dabat', 'gave from her mouth', a full epic way of saying 'spoke'. Elisions 'Veloc(em) interea', 'un(am) ex'.

sentences.t:
“Graditur bellum ad crudele Camilla,
O virgo, et nostris nequiquam cingitur armis,
cara mihi ante alias.
sentences.l:
“Is marching to war, the cruel, Camilla,
O maiden, and girds herself in vain with our arms,
dear to me before others.”
sentences.i: “Camilla is marching to a cruel war, maiden, and arms herself in vain with weapons of ours; she is dear to me above all others.”
sentences.n: The print has 'alias. ”Neque', the closing mark joined to the next word, a misprint for 'alias.” Neque', corrected here (as 'vale. ”Nec', 11.98). In the print Diana's first words end here and resume at 'Vellem' (584–594); between, the poet tells Camilla's story. Many editors give all of 535–594 to Diana; either reading is possible, so the print's marks are kept. 'Graditur', 'steps, marches', put first, with the name held to the end of the line. 'nostris… armis', 'with our arms', the bow and quiver that are Diana's own weapons. 'nequiquam', 'in vain', tells the reader at once that Camilla will die. 'cingitur', passive in middle sense, 'girds herself'. 'cara mihi ante alias', 'dear to me before other women', 'alias' feminine. Elisions 'bell(um) ad', 'virg(o) et', 'mih(i) ante', 'ant(e) alias'.

sentences.t:
”Neque enim novus iste Dianae
venit amor subitaque animum dulcedine movit.
sentences.l:
For not new this of Diana
has come love, nor with a sudden sweetness has it moved her heart.
sentences.i: For this love of Diana's is no new thing, nor has it stirred her heart with a sudden sweetness.
sentences.n: The closing speech mark printed at the head of this unit belongs to Diana's words before it (see the note there). With the print's marks the poet now speaks, naming the goddess, 'Dianae'. Others keep Diana speaking: 'enim' and 'iste' sound like speech, gods name themselves (compare 582), and 'Vellem' (584) needs no verb of speaking. 'Neque enim', 'for… not'. 'novus… amor', framing; 'venit', perfect, 'has come': the metre needs the long 'vē-'. 'subita… dulcedine', 'with sudden sweetness', a passing fancy. 'animum', hers. Elisions 'Nequ(e) enim', 'subitaqu(e) animum'.

sentences.t:
Pulsus ob invidiam regno viresque superbas
Priverno antiqua Metabus cum excederet urbe,
infantem fugiens media inter proelia belli
sustulit exsilio comitem matrisque vocavit
nomine Casmillae mutata parte Camillam.
sentences.l:
Driven, on account of hatred, from his kingdom, and of his proud strength,
from Privernum, the ancient, when Metabus was departing, the city,
the infant, fleeing in the midst of the battles of war,
he took up as a companion for exile, and of her mother called her
by the name, Casmilla, one part changed, Camilla.
sentences.i: When Metabus was driven from his throne because of the hatred his overbearing power had stirred, and was leaving the ancient city of Privernum, he took up his baby daughter in his flight, in the thick of the fighting, to share his exile, and named her Camilla, after her mother Casmilla, with one part of the name changed.
sentences.n: 'Pulsus… regno', 'driven from his kingdom', ablative of separation. 'ob' governs both 'invidiam' and 'vires… superbas': 'because of hatred and his proud strength', in effect 'the hatred his tyranny roused'. 'Priverno… urbe', 'from the city of Privernum', a Volscian town in the hills south-east of Rome. 'cum excederet', 'when he was leaving'. 'sustulit', perfect of 'tollo', 'took up', as a father lifted a newborn to acknowledge it. 'matris… nomine Casmillae', 'by her mother's name, Casmilla', 'mutata parte', the 's' dropped. Servius connects 'camillus, camilla', a boy or girl who served a priest. Elisions 'Privern(o) antiqua', 'cu(m) excederet', 'medi(a) inter'.

sentences.t:
Ipse sinu prae se portans iuga longa petebat
solorum nemorum:
sentences.l:
He himself, in the fold of his robe before him carrying her, the long ridges was seeking
of lonely woods:
sentences.i: He himself made for the long ridges of the lonely forests, carrying her before him in the fold of his robe:
sentences.n: 'Ipse', Metabus, alone, with no one to carry the child for him. 'sinu', 'in the fold of his garment', the loose fold of cloth across the chest. 'prae se', 'in front of him'. 'iuga longa… solorum nemorum', 'the long ridges of lonely woods', the empty uplands where a fugitive might hide. 'petebat', the imperfect of an action in progress, interrupted in the lines that follow. No elisions.

sentences.t:
tela undique saeva premebant
et circumfuso volitabant milite Volsci.
sentences.l:
weapons on every side, cruel, were pressing,
and with soldiery poured around were flitting about the Volsci.
sentences.i: cruel weapons pressed on him from every side, and the Volscians darted all around him with their troops spread about him.
sentences.n: 'tela… saeva premebant', 'cruel weapons were pressing (him)', the weapons for the men who threw them. 'circumfuso… milite', 'with soldiery poured round', an ablative of manner or attendant circumstance; 'miles' is collective. 'volitabant', frequentative of 'volo', 'fly', 'kept flitting about', the pursuers moving swiftly round him. The 'Volsci' are his own people, now his enemies. Elision 'tel(a) undique'.

sentences.t:
Ecce fugae medio summis Amasenus abundans
spumabat ripis:
sentences.l:
Look, in the middle of the flight, at the tops, Amasenus, overflowing,
was foaming of its banks:
sentences.i: See, there in the midst of his flight the Amasenus was foaming over, brimming to the tops of its banks:
sentences.n: 'Ecce', 'look!', the storyteller's call to see the sudden obstacle. 'fugae medio', 'in the middle of the flight', 'medio' a neuter noun with the genitive. The Amasenus is a river of the Volscian country that runs past Privernum down to the Pomptine marshes. 'summis… ripis', 'at the tops of its banks', framing 'Amasenus abundans'. 'abundans', from 'ab' and 'unda', 'streaming off in waves', overflowing. 'spumabat', foaming with the flood. No elisions.

sentences.t:
tantus se nubibus imber
ruperat.
sentences.l:
so great from the clouds a rain
had burst.
sentences.i: so heavy a rain had broken from the clouds.
sentences.n: 'tantus… imber', 'so great a downpour', framing the clause. 'se… ruperat', 'had burst itself', a reflexive verb used where English uses an intransitive: the rain broke out of the clouds. 'nubibus', ablative of separation, 'from the clouds'. The pluperfect explains the flood: the storm had come before Metabus reached the river. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Ille, innare parans, infantis amore
tardatur caroque oneri timet.
sentences.l:
He, to swim in preparing, by love of the infant
is held back, and for his dear burden he fears.
sentences.i: He was ready to swim across, but love for the child held him back, and he feared for his precious burden.
sentences.n: 'Ille', Metabus. 'innare parans', 'preparing to swim in', the river being the obstacle. 'infantis amore', 'by love of the infant', objective genitive. 'tardatur', 'is slowed', the historic present, as often in vivid narrative. 'caro… oneri timet', 'fears for his dear burden', 'timeo' with the dative of the person or thing one fears for. Elisions 'Ill(e) innare', 'caroqu(e) oneri'.

sentences.t:
Omnia secum
versanti subito vix haec sententia sedit.
sentences.l:
All things with himself
to him turning over, suddenly, scarcely, this decision settled.
sentences.i: As he turned every course over in his mind, all at once, and barely, this plan took hold.
sentences.n: 'Omnia secum versanti', 'to him turning everything over with himself', dative of the person concerned, depending loosely on 'sedit': the decision settled 'for him'. 'secum', 'with himself', 'in his own mind'. 'subito vix', 'suddenly, (and) hardly': the plan came all at once, and he could barely bring himself to it. 'sententia sedit', 'the resolve was fixed', as a judge's sentence settles. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Telum immane manu valida quod forte gerebat
bellator, solidum nodis et robore cocto,
huic natam, libro et silvestri subere clausam,
implicat atque habilem mediae circumligat hastae;
sentences.l:
A weapon huge, which in his strong hand by chance he was carrying,
a warrior, solid with knots and oak seasoned by fire,
to this his daughter, in bark and woodland cork enclosed,
he ties, and, handily, round the middle he binds of the spear;
sentences.i: He was a warrior, and he happened to be carrying in his strong hand a huge spear, solid with knots and fire-hardened oak; to this he tied his daughter, wrapped in bark and the cork of the woodland oak, and lashed her, well balanced, round the middle of the shaft;
sentences.n: The sentence begins with the spear, 'Telum immane', drawn into the relative clause as the object of 'gerebat' ('a huge spear, which…'), and picks it up again with 'huic' and 'hastae', a loose but vivid order. 'bellator', 'as a warrior', in apposition to the subject. 'robore cocto', 'oak baked', hardened in the fire. 'libro', from 'liber', 'inner bark'; 'subere', 'cork', from the cork-oak. 'habilem', 'handy', set so the spear balances. 'mediae… hastae', dative with 'circumligat'. Elisions 'Tel(um) immane', 'libr(o) et', 'atqu(e) habilem'.

sentences.t: quam dextra ingenti librans ita ad aethera fatur:
sentences.l: which in his huge right hand balancing, thus to the sky he speaks:
sentences.i: then, poising it in his mighty right hand, he spoke thus to the heavens:
sentences.n: 'quam', connecting relative, 'and this (spear)'. 'librans', 'balancing, poising', the thrower's weighing of the shaft before the cast. 'dextra ingenti', 'in his huge right hand'. 'ad aethera', 'to the upper air', Greek accusative 'aethera'. 'fatur', the deponent 'for', 'speaks', in the historic present. Metabus's prayer follows, in speech marks of its own. Elisions 'dextr(a) ingenti', 'it(a) ad'.

sentences.t:
“Alma, tibi hanc, nemorum cultrix, Latonia virgo,
ipse pater famulam voveo; tua prima per auras
tela tenens supplex hostem fugit.
sentences.l:
“Kindly one, to you this one, of the groves dweller, Latona's maiden daughter,
I myself, her father, as a servant vow; your first through the airs
weapons holding, a suppliant she flees the enemy.
sentences.i: “Kind goddess, maiden daughter of Latona, who dwell among the groves, I her father vow this child to you as your handmaid; the first weapons she ever holds are yours, as she flies through the air, your suppliant, from the enemy.
sentences.n: Metabus's prayer begins. (On the reading that gives the whole story to Diana, see 537, it would be a speech within her speech.) 'Alma', 'nourishing, kindly', a cult title. 'nemorum cultrix', 'dweller in the groves', Diana's haunts. 'tibi hanc… famulam voveo', 'I vow this one to you as your servant', a formal vow. 'ipse pater', the father who may dispose of his child. 'tua prima… tela tenens', 'holding your weapons as her first': the spear is Diana's, the huntress's, and the first she grasps. Elision 'tib(i) hanc'.

sentences.t:
Accipe, testor,
diva tuam, quae nunc dubiis committitur auris.”
sentences.l:
Receive, I beseech,
goddess, as your own, who now is entrusted to the doubtful breezes.”
sentences.i: Receive her, goddess, I implore you, as your own, for she is now entrusted to the uncertain winds.”
sentences.n: Metabus's prayer ends. 'Accipe', 'receive', the word of a god accepting an offering. 'testor', 'I call (you) to witness', here 'I implore'. 'diva tuam', 'goddess, (her as) your own', the two words set side by side. 'dubiis… auris', 'to the doubtful airs', framing 'committitur', 'is entrusted'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Dixit et adducto contortum hastile lacerto
immittit:
sentences.l:
He spoke, and with arm drawn back the whirled spear-shaft
he sends:
sentences.i: He spoke, drew back his arm, and sent the spear spinning on its way:
sentences.n: 'Dixit', the closing formula of a speech, 'he spoke'. 'adducto… lacerto', ablative absolute, 'the upper arm drawn back', the throwing arm cocked. 'contortum hastile', 'the shaft whirled', given spin in the throw. 'immittit', 'sends at, launches', the historic present after the perfect. Elision 'contort(um) hastile'.

sentences.t:
sonuere undae, rapidum super amnem
infelix fugit in iaculo stridente Camilla.
sentences.l:
roared the waters, over the rapid river
unhappy flees on the whistling javelin Camilla.
sentences.i: the waters roared, and over the racing river poor Camilla flew on the whistling javelin.
sentences.n: 'sonuere' = 'sonuerunt', the perfect in '-ere' (you will meet it constantly). 'rapidum super amnem', 'over the swift river', 'super' placed between adjective and noun. 'infelix', 'unhappy, ill-starred', pity for a child whose life began in flight and will end in war. 'fugit', 'flees, flies', as the spear carries her. 'stridente', 'hissing, whistling', the sound of the shaft in flight. Elision 'sonuer(e) undae'.

sentences.t:
At Metabus, magna propius iam urgente caterva,
dat sese fluvio atque hastam cum virgine victor
gramineo donum Triviae de caespite vellit.
sentences.l:
But Metabus, the great band now nearer pressing,
gives himself to the river and the spear with the maiden, victorious,
from the grassy, a gift to Trivia, turf plucks out.
sentences.i: But Metabus, now that the great band was pressing closer, plunged into the river, and on the other side, triumphant, pulled the spear with the girl on it, his gift to Trivia, out of the grassy turf.
sentences.n: 'magna… caterva', ablative absolute with 'urgente', 'the great band pressing'. 'dat sese fluvio', 'gives himself to the river', plunges in. 'victor', 'victorious', over the flood and his pursuers. 'gramineo… de caespite', 'from the grassy turf', where the spear has stuck. 'donum Triviae', in apposition: the child is now Diana's. 'Trivia', 'goddess of the crossroads', a title of Diana as one with Hecate. Elisions 'i(am) urgente', 'fluvi(o) atque', 'atqu(e) hastam'.

sentences.t:
Non illum tectis ullae, non moenibus urbes
accepere neque ipse manus feritate dedisset:
sentences.l:
Not him into houses did any, not within walls, cities
receive, nor would he himself in his wildness have given his hands:
sentences.i: No city took him in under its roofs or within its walls, nor, in his wild pride, would he himself have yielded:
sentences.n: 'Non… ullae, non… urbes', 'no cities… none', the double negation hammering home his isolation. 'tectis… moenibus', datives or ablatives, 'into houses, within walls'. 'accepere' = 'acceperunt'. 'manus dare', 'to give one's hands', to surrender, as a captive holds out his hands to be bound: Metabus would not have bowed to any city. 'feritate', ablative of cause, 'in his wildness'. Elision 'nequ(e) ipse'.

sentences.t: pastorum et solis exegit montibus aevom.
sentences.l: Among the shepherds' and the lonely mountains he passed his life.
sentences.i: He spent his days among the lonely mountains where only shepherds go.
sentences.n: 'pastorum et solis… montibus', 'on the mountains of shepherds and lonely', 'et' joining a genitive and an adjective: the mountains belong to herdsmen and are empty of towns. 'exegit', 'drove out, spent', of a lifetime. 'aevom', Greenough's old spelling of 'aevum', 'lifetime', keeping the early 'o' after 'v', as in 'divom' and 'volnus'. Elision 'pastor(um) et'.

sentences.t:
Hic natam in dumis interque horrentia lustra
armentalis equae mammis et lacte ferino
nutribat, teneris immulgens ubera labris.
sentences.l:
Here his daughter in thickets and among the bristling lairs
of a herd-mare at the teats and with milk wild
he nourished, milking the udders into her tender lips.
sentences.i: Here, among thorn-brakes and the bristling lairs of wild beasts, he reared his daughter on the teats of a mare from the herd and on wild creatures' milk, milking the udders into her tender lips.
sentences.n: 'in dumis… horrentia lustra', 'in thickets… bristling dens', the haunts of wild animals. 'armentalis equae', 'of a mare of the herd', a brood mare running half-wild in the hills. 'lacte ferino', 'with milk of wild beasts': the story recalls the she-wolf that suckled Romulus and Remus. 'nutribat' = 'nutriebat', the old imperfect of a fourth-conjugation verb. 'immulgens', 'milking into', a rare compound. 'teneris… labris', framing 'immulgens ubera'. Elisions 'nat(am) in', 'interqu(e) horrentia'.

sentences.t:
Utque pedum primis infans vestigia plantis
institerat, iaculo palmas armavit acuto
spiculaque ex umero parvae suspendit et arcum.
sentences.l:
And when, of her feet with the first soles, the infant footprints
had set, with a javelin her palms he armed, a sharp one,
and arrows from the shoulder of the little one hung, and a bow.
sentences.i: And as soon as the child had planted her first footsteps with the soles of her feet, he armed her hands with a sharp javelin and hung arrows and a bow from the little girl's shoulder.
sentences.n: 'Utque', 'and as soon as', 'ut' with the pluperfect 'institerat', 'had stood on'. 'pedum primis… vestigia plantis', 'footprints with the first soles of her feet', a fond, elaborate way of saying 'when she first walked'. 'iaculo… acuto', framing 'palmas armavit'. 'spicula', 'arrows', with 'arcum' added at the end. 'parvae', dative, 'from the little one's shoulder'. Elision 'spiculaqu(e) ex'.

sentences.t:
Pro crinali auro, pro longae tegmine pallae
tigridis exuviae per dorsum a vertice pendent.
sentences.l:
Instead of hair-gold, instead of a long robe's covering,
a tiger's spoils down her back from the crown of her head hang.
sentences.i: Instead of gold in her hair and the covering of a long robe, a tiger's skin hangs from her head down her back.
sentences.n: 'Pro… pro', 'instead of… instead of', the anaphora setting what a girl of her birth should wear against what she does wear. 'crinali auro', 'hair-gold', gold pins or a net for the hair. 'palla', the long mantle of a grown woman. 'tigridis exuviae', 'a tigress's spoils', the stripped skin; the tiger is an exotic touch for Italy. The present 'pendent' brings the picture before our eyes. Elisions 'crinal(i) auro', 'dors(um) a'.

sentences.t:
Tela manu iam tum tenera puerilia torsit
et fundam tereti circum caput egit habena
Strymoniamque gruem aut album deiecit olorem.
sentences.l:
Weapons with her hand already then tender childish she hurled,
and the sling round her head she drove by its smooth thong,
and a Strymonian crane or a white swan brought down.
sentences.i: Even then she was hurling a child's darts with her tender hand and whirling a sling round her head on its smooth thong, and bringing down a Strymonian crane or a white swan.
sentences.n: 'iam tum', 'even then', while still a child. 'tela… puerilia', 'childish weapons', framing; 'manu… tenera', 'with tender hand'. 'fundam… egit', 'drove the sling round', whirled it. 'tereti… habena', 'with a smooth thong', framing 'circum caput'. 'Strymoniam… gruem', 'a Strymonian crane', from the Strymon in Thrace, where cranes gathered in poetry. 'olor', 'swan', a poetic word. Elision 'gru(em) aut'.

sentences.t:
Multae illam frustra Tyrrhena per oppida matres
optavere nurum:
sentences.l:
Many her in vain through the Tyrrhenian towns mothers
wished for as daughter-in-law:
sentences.i: Many a mother through the towns of Etruria longed in vain to have her as a son's bride:
sentences.n: 'Multae… matres', framing the line. 'illam… optavere nurum', 'wished for her as daughter-in-law', 'nurum' predicative. 'optavere' = 'optaverunt'. 'Tyrrhena… oppida', the Etruscan towns, in whose country the Volscian exile lived near the border; mothers chose wives for their sons. 'frustra', 'in vain', held early. Elision 'Mult(ae) illam'.

sentences.t:
sola contenta Diana
aeternum telorum et virginitatis amorem
intemerata colit.
sentences.l:
alone content with Diana,
an eternal love of weapons and of maidenhood
undefiled she cherishes.
sentences.i: content with Diana alone, she cherishes, unsullied, an undying love for weapons and for maidenhood.
sentences.n: 'sola contenta Diana', 'content with Diana alone', ablative with 'contenta': 'sola' is ablative here, agreeing with 'Diana'. The goddess is named again, as at 537. 'aeternum… amorem', framing 'telorum et virginitatis'. 'intemerata', 'unviolated', a solemn word. 'colit', 'cherishes', also used of tending a cult. The present tense: Camilla is still a virgin huntress now. Elision 'telor(um) et'.

sentences.t:
“Vellem haud correpta fuisset
militia tali, conata lacessere Teucros:
sentences.l:
“I would wish she had not been seized
by warfare such, having tried to provoke the Teucrians:
sentences.i: “I could wish she had never been swept up into such a war, or tried to challenge the Trojans:
sentences.n: Diana speaks again, with the print's opening mark before 'Vellem', and goes on to 594 (on the marks, see 537). 'Vellem… correpta fuisset', 'I would wish she had not been seized', an unfulfillable wish for the past: 'vellem' with the pluperfect subjunctive, 'ut' left out. 'correpta… militia tali', 'carried off by such soldiering'. 'conata', 'having tried'. 'Teucros', 'Teucrians', the Trojans. Elision 'Vell(em) haud'.

sentences.t: cara mihi comitumque foret nunc una mearum.
sentences.l: dear to me and of my companions she would be now one.
sentences.i: she would still be dear to me, and one of my companions.
sentences.n: 'foret', an old form equal to 'esset', the imperfect subjunctive of 'sum': the apodosis of the wish, 'she would (now) be'. 'cara mihi', picking up 535–537. 'comitum… una mearum', 'one of my companions', the genitive split around 'foret nunc'. The point is that she is dear now and will soon be lost. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Verum age, quandoquidem fatis urgetur acerbis,
abere, nympha, polo finisque invise Latinos,
tristis ubi infausto committitur omine pugna.
sentences.l:
But come, since by fates she is pressed bitter,
glide down, nymph, from the sky, and the borders visit Latin,
where the sad fight is joined under an unlucky omen.
sentences.i: But come, since bitter fate bears hard upon her, glide down from heaven, nymph, and go to the Latin lands, where a grim battle is being joined under evil omens.
sentences.n: The print has 'abere', a misprint for 'labere', corrected here. 'labere', imperative of the deponent 'labor', 'glide, slip down', the gods' swift descent. 'Verum age', 'but come', turning to action. 'quandoquidem', 'since in fact'. 'fatis… acerbis', 'by bitter fates', framing 'urgetur'. 'polo', 'from the sky', ablative of separation. 'finis… Latinos', '-is' accusative plural. 'tristis… pugna', framing; 'committitur', 'is joined'. Elisions 'Ver(um) age', 'finisqu(e) invise', 'ub(i) infausto'.

sentences.t: Haec cape et ultricem pharetra deprome sagittam:
sentences.l: These take, and an avenging from the quiver draw out arrow:
sentences.i: Take these, and draw from the quiver an arrow of vengeance:
sentences.n: 'Haec cape', 'take these', with a gesture: Diana hands Opis her bow and quiver. 'ultricem… sagittam', 'an avenging arrow', framing the line; 'ultrix' is the feminine of 'ultor', 'avenger'. 'pharetra', ablative of separation, 'from the quiver'. 'deprome', 'take out', a compound of 'promo'. Elision 'cap(e) et'.

sentences.t:
hac quicumque sacrum violarit volnere corpus,
Tros Italusque, mihi pariter det sanguine poenas.
sentences.l:
with this, whoever the sacred violates with a wound body,
Trojan or Italian, to me equally let him give with blood the penalty.
sentences.i: with this let whoever wounds and violates her sacred body, Trojan or Italian, pay me alike the price in his blood.
sentences.n: 'hac', 'with this (arrow)'. 'violarit' = 'violaverit', the future perfect contracted, 'shall have violated'. 'sacrum… corpus', framing 'violarit volnere': Camilla's body is sacred as Diana's votary. 'volnere', Greenough's spelling of 'vulnere'. 'Tros Italusque', 'Trojan or Italian', '-que' with the force of '-ve': whichever side. 'det… poenas', 'let him pay the penalty', jussive. 'sanguine', 'with his blood'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Post ego nube cava miserandae corpus et arma
inspoliata feram tumulo patriaeque reponam.”
sentences.l:
Afterwards I, in a hollow cloud, of the pitiable one the body and arms
unspoiled will carry to the tomb and lay back in her homeland.”
sentences.i: Afterwards I myself, wrapped in a hollow cloud, will carry the poor girl's body and her arms, unplundered, to the tomb, and lay them to rest in her own country.”
sentences.n: Diana's speech ends. 'Post ego', 'afterwards I (myself)'. 'nube cava', 'in a hollow cloud', the gods' way of hiding and carrying. 'miserandae', gerundive, 'of the girl to be pitied'. 'inspoliata', 'unspoiled', not stripped by the victor, as armour usually was. 'tumulo', dative of goal, 'to the burial mound'. 'patriae… reponam', 'restore to her homeland'. In the Iliad Sleep and Death carry the dead Sarpedon home to Lycia, a scene Virgil may have in mind. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Dixit; at illa levis caeli delapsa per auras
insonuit, nigro circumdata turbine corpus.
sentences.l:
She spoke; but she, light, of heaven slipping down through the airs,
sounded, wrapped about in a black whirlwind as to her body.
sentences.i: She spoke; and the nymph, gliding lightly down through the airs of heaven, went rushing and resounding, her body wrapped in a dark whirlwind.
sentences.n: 'Dixit', the closing formula. 'at illa', 'but she', the other one, Opis. 'levis', 'light', nominative, of her swift and weightless descent. 'delapsa', from 'delabor', 'having glided down': she obeys 'labere' at 588. 'insonuit', 'made a sound', the rush of her passage. 'circumdata corpus', 'wrapped as to her body', the accusative with a passive participle in middle sense. 'nigro… turbine', framing. No elisions.

sentences.t:
At manus interea muris Troiana propinquat
Etruscique duces equitumque exercitus omnis,
compositi numero in turmas.
sentences.l:
But the force meanwhile to the walls Trojan approaches,
and the Etruscan leaders and of horsemen the army whole,
arranged by number in squadrons.
sentences.i: Meanwhile the Trojan force was coming near the walls, with the Etruscan leaders and the whole host of horse, drawn up in squadrons of equal number.
sentences.n: A new paragraph in Greenough, back on earth. 'manus… Troiana', 'the Trojan band', framing. 'muris', dative with 'propinquat', 'approaches the walls'. 'propinquat' is singular with three subjects, agreeing with the nearest; 'compositi' then shifts to the plural by sense, the men. 'numero in turmas', 'into squadrons by number', in equal troops. Elisions 'equitumqu(e) exercitus', 'numer(o) in'.

sentences.i: Over the whole plain the charger snorts and prances, and fights against the tightened rein, swinging this way and that;
sentences.n: 'Fremit', 'roars, snorts', put first. 'aequore toto', 'over the whole level', 'aequor', any flat expanse, here the plain. 'insultans', 'leaping on, prancing'. 'sonipes', 'sound-foot', a poetic word for a horse, used collectively for all the horses. 'pressis… habenis', ablative absolute, 'with reins held tight'; 'pugnat', 'fights', strains against them. 'huc… et huc', 'this way and this', to and fro. No elisions.

sentences.t:
tum late ferreus hastis
horret ager campique armis sublimibus ardent.
sentences.l:
then far and wide iron with spears
bristles the field and the plains with arms raised blaze.
sentences.i: then far and wide the field bristles with iron spears, and the plains glitter with weapons held aloft.
sentences.n: 'ferreus hastis… ager', 'the field iron with spears', framing: the spear-points make the field look like iron. 'horret', 'bristles', the word for hair standing on end, used of a field of spears, as of a cornfield. 'armis sublimibus', 'with arms held high'. 'ardent', 'blaze', of the flashing metal. Elision 'campiqu(e) armis'.

sentences.t:
Nec non Messapus contra celeresque Latini
et cum fratre Coras et virginis ala Camillae
adversi campo apparent hastasque reductis
protendunt longe dextris et spicula vibrant,
adventusque virum fremitusque ardescit equorum.
sentences.l:
Likewise Messapus opposite, and the swift Latins,
and with his brother Coras, and of the maiden the wing, Camilla,
facing on the plain appear, and spears with drawn-back
they thrust out far right hands, and javelins they brandish,
and the approach of men and the snorting grows hot of horses.
sentences.i: On the other side Messapus and the swift Latins, Coras with his brother, and the maiden Camilla's wing appear across the plain, facing them, and with right arms drawn back they thrust their spears far out and brandish their javelins, and the advance of men and the snorting of horses grow fiercer.
sentences.n: 'Nec non', 'and also', two negatives making a positive. Messapus is the horse-tamer, son of Neptune, of VII.691; Coras's brother is Catillus, the twins from Tibur (VII.670–672). 'virginis ala Camillae', 'the wing of the maiden Camilla', 'ala' the cavalry term. 'adversi', 'facing (them)'. 'reductis… dextris', 'with right hands drawn back', framing the spear-thrust. 'virum', old genitive plural, 'of men'. 'ardescit', singular with two subjects, 'catches fire'. Elisions 'camp(o) apparent', 'fremitusqu(e) ardescit'.

sentences.t:
Iamque intra iactum teli progressus uterque
substiterat:
sentences.l:
And now within the throw of a weapon having advanced each side
had halted:
sentences.i: And now each side had advanced to within a spear's throw and halted:
sentences.n: 'intra iactum teli', 'within the cast of a spear', the distance at which battle begins. 'uterque', 'each of the two', the two armies, with a singular verb. 'progressus… substiterat', 'having advanced, had come to a stand', the pluperfect marking a pause before the sudden 'subito' that follows. Elision 'Iamqu(e) intra'.

sentences.t:
subito erumpunt clamore furentisque
exhortantur equos;
sentences.l:
suddenly they burst out with a shout, and the raging
they urge on, horses;
sentences.i: suddenly they broke forward with a shout and urged on their maddened horses;
sentences.n: 'erumpunt', 'they burst out', the historic present. 'clamore', 'with a shout', the battle cry. 'furentis… equos', '-is' accusative plural, 'raging horses'. The line ends in 'furentisque', and it has a syllable too many: the '-que' is elided into 'exhortantur' at the start of the next line. This 'hypermetric' line is rare in Virgil and usually suggests overflow, here of the charge. Elision 'subit(o) erumpunt'.

sentences.t:
fundunt simul undique tela
crebra nivis ritu caelumque obtexitur umbra.
sentences.l:
they pour together from all sides weapons
thick in the manner of snow, and the sky is covered with shadow.
sentences.i: from every side together they pour out showers of weapons, thick as snow, and the sky is darkened with their shadow.
sentences.n: 'fundunt… tela', 'they pour weapons', as if liquid. 'simul undique', 'at once from everywhere'. 'crebra nivis ritu', 'thick in the manner of snow', 'ritu' with the genitive meaning 'like'; in the Iliad stones and missiles fall like snowflakes. 'obtexitur', 'is woven over', a covering of missiles that hides the light. Elision 'caelumqu(e) obtexitur'.

sentences.t:
Continuo adversis Tyrrhenus et acer Aconteus
conixi incurrunt hastis primique ruina
dant sonitum ingenti perfractaque quadrupedantum
pectora pectoribus rumpunt:
sentences.l:
At once with opposed, Tyrrhenus and keen Aconteus,
straining, charge spears, and first, with a crash
huge, give a sound, and the shattered of the gallopers
chests with chests they break:
sentences.i: At once Tyrrhenus and fierce Aconteus, straining, charged at each other with levelled spears, and were the first to raise a din, crashing down mightily, and the chests of their horses broke and shattered against each other:
sentences.n: 'Tyrrhenus', an Etruscan on the Trojan side, against 'Aconteus', a Latin. 'adversis… hastis', 'with spears opposed'. 'conixi', from 'conitor', 'having strained'. 'ruina… ingenti', 'with a huge crash', framing 'dant sonitum'; the Latin Library reads 'ruinam dant sonitu ingenti', 'make a fall with a huge sound', but the print makes good sense and is kept. 'quadrupedantum', old genitive plural, 'of the galloping ones', the horses. 'pectora pectoribus', the repetition for the collision. Elisions 'Continu(o) adversis', 'conix(i) incurrunt', 'sonit(um) ingenti'.

sentences.t:
excussus Aconteus
fulminis in morem aut tormento ponderis acti
praecipitat longe et vitam dispergit in auras.
sentences.l:
thrown off, Aconteus,
like a thunderbolt or by an engine of a weight driven,
plunges headlong far and his life scatters into the airs.
sentences.i: Aconteus was flung off like a thunderbolt or a stone shot from a war-engine, and was hurled far away headlong, scattering his life on the winds.
sentences.n: 'excussus', 'shaken out', thrown from the saddle. 'fulminis in morem', 'in the manner of a thunderbolt', and 'in morem' governs the second genitive too: 'or (of) a weight driven by a catapult', 'tormento' the ablative of means. 'praecipitat', intransitive, 'falls headlong'. 'vitam dispergit in auras', 'scatters his life into the air': the life thought of as breath. Elisions 'mor(em) aut', 'long(e) et'.

sentences.t:
Extemplo turbatae acies, versique Latini
reiciunt parmas et equos ad moenia vertunt.
sentences.l:
Immediately thrown into confusion the lines, and turned the Latins
throw back their shields and their horses to the walls turn.
sentences.i: At once the ranks were thrown into disorder, and the Latins wheeled about, slung their shields on their backs and turned their horses toward the walls.
sentences.n: 'turbatae (sunt) acies', with the verb left out. 'versi', 'turned', in flight. 'reiciunt parmas', 'throw back their small shields', slinging them over their backs to guard them as they flee. 'parma', the round cavalry shield. 'reiciunt' scans with its first syllable long, as if 'reiiciunt', a consonantal 'i' after a prefix. 'ad moenia', to the Latin city. Elision 'turbat(ae) acies'.

sentences.t: Troes agunt, princeps turmas inducit Asilas.
sentences.l: The Trojans drive them, first leads in the squadrons Asilas.
sentences.i: The Trojans pursued, and Asilas led the squadrons in at their head.
sentences.n: 'Troes', Greek nominative plural, two syllables, Trō-es, 'Trojans', here the whole Trojan and Etruscan force. 'agunt', 'drive (them)', in pursuit. 'princeps', 'foremost', in apposition: Asilas leads the charge. Asilas is the Etruscan seer and captain named in the catalogue of Aeneas's allies (X.175). 'inducit', 'leads in', against the enemy. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Iamque propinquabant portis, rursusque Latini
clamorem tollunt et mollia colla reflectunt:
sentences.l:
And now they were approaching the gates, and again the Latins
a shout raise and the pliant necks bend back:
sentences.i: And now they were nearing the gates, when the Latins raised a shout once more and wheeled their horses' supple necks around:
sentences.n: 'propinquabant', imperfect, 'were getting near'; the subject is the pursuing Trojans. 'portis', dative. 'rursus', 'again', 'back': the Latins rally. 'clamorem tollunt', 'raise a shout'. 'mollia colla reflectunt', 'bend back the pliant necks', of their horses, turning them to face the enemy. No elisions.

sentences.t: hi fugiunt penitusque datis referuntur habenis.
sentences.l: these flee, and far are carried back with given reins.
sentences.i: and now it was the others who fled, carried far back at full gallop.
sentences.n: 'hi', 'these', now the Trojans and Etruscans, turning to flee. 'penitus', 'far, deep', 'right back'. 'datis… habenis', ablative absolute, 'with reins given', given free rein, at full speed. 'referuntur', 'are carried back', passive in middle sense. The tide turns; the simile follows. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Qualis ubi alterno procurrens gurgite pontus
nunc ruit ad terram scopulusque superiacit unda
spumeus extremamque sinu perfundit arenam,
nunc rapidus retro atque aestu revoluta resorbens
saxa fugit litusque vado labente relinquit:
sentences.l:
As when, with alternating running forward flood, the sea
now rushes to the land and the rocks overtops with its wave,
foaming, and the farthest with its curve drenches sand,
now swift backward and, by the surge rolled back, sucking in
the stones it flees, and the shore, with the shallow sliding, leaves:
sentences.i: As when the sea comes running in with alternating flood, and now rushes at the land, flinging its foaming wave over the rocks and drenching the farthest sand in its curving sweep, and now flees swiftly backward, sucking down the stones that its surge has rolled, and leaves the shore as the shallows slide away:
sentences.n: The print has 'scopulusque', a misprint for 'scopulosque', corrected here (the Latin Library has 'scopulosque'): 'superiacit', 'throws over', needs an object, and 'spumeus' goes with 'pontus'; a nominative 'scopulus' would leave the verb with no object and make the crag the thrower. 'Qualis ubi', 'as when', opening the simile. 'alterno… gurgite', 'with alternating flood', the tide's ebb and flow. 'unda', ablative, 'with its wave'. 'sinu', 'with its curve'. 'arenam', Greenough's spelling of 'harenam'. 'revoluta… saxa', 'the stones rolled back'. 'vado labente', ablative absolute. Elisions 'ub(i) alterno', 'retr(o) atque', 'atqu(e) aestu'.

sentences.t:
bis Tusci Rutulos egere ad moenia versos,
bis reiecti armis respectant terga tegentes.
sentences.l:
Twice the Tuscans the Rutulians drove to the walls, turned,
twice, thrown back, they look behind, their backs with arms covering.
sentences.i: Twice the Etruscans drove the Rutulians routed to the walls; twice they were thrown back in their turn, and looked behind them as they fled, covering their backs with their shields.
sentences.n: The simile applied: the two 'bis' clauses are the advance and the ebb. 'Tusci', the Etruscans; 'Rutulos', Turnus's people, standing for all the Latin side. 'egere' = 'egerunt'. 'versos', 'turned', in flight. In the second clause 'reiecti' is most naturally the Etruscans, thrown back in turn, though some take it of the Rutulians. 'respectant', frequentative, 'keep looking back'. 'terga tegentes', 'covering their backs' with shields. Elisions 'eger(e) ad', 'reiect(i) armis'.

sentences.t:
Tertia sed postquam congressi in proelia totas
implicuere inter se acies legitque virum vir:
sentences.l:
The third but after, meeting, into battles, the whole
they entangled with each other lines, and picked man man:
sentences.i: But when they met for the third time and the whole lines locked together, and man singled out man:
sentences.n: 'Tertia… in proelia', 'into the third battle', the plural used for a single clash. 'sed postquam', with 'sed' postponed. 'congressi', 'having come together'. 'implicuere' = 'implicuerunt', 'entangled'. 'totas… acies', 'the whole lines'. 'legit… virum vir', 'man chose man', 'lēgit' perfect (the metre needs the long e), each picking his opponent; here 'virum' is the accusative singular, not the old genitive plural of 607. Elisions 'congress(i) in', 'implicuer(e) inter', 's(e) acies'.

sentences.t:
tum vero et gemitus morientum et sanguine in alto
armaque corporaque et permixti caede virorum
semianimes volvuntur equi, pugna aspera surgit.
sentences.l:
then indeed both the groans of the dying, and in blood deep
both arms and bodies and, mingled with the slaughter of men,
half-alive roll horses, the fight harsh rises.
sentences.i: then indeed the groans of the dying rose, and in deep blood weapons and bodies and half-dead horses rolled, mixed up with the slaughter of men, and a savage fight broke out.
sentences.n: 'tum vero', 'then indeed', after 'postquam'. 'gemitus morientum', 'groans of the dying', 'morientum' the old genitive plural for 'morientium'; 'gemitus' shares 'volvuntur' with the arms, bodies and horses, a bold zeugma (the groans 'roll' out); some supply 'rise' instead. 'sanguine in alto', 'in deep blood'. 'armaque corporaque', the double '-que'. 'permixti caede virorum', 'mixed with the slaughter of men'. 'semianimes', four syllables, the 'i' consonantal. 'pugna aspera surgit', in asyndeton. Elisions 'ver(o) et', 'morient(um) et', 'sanguin(e) in', 'corporaqu(e) et', 'pugn(a) aspera'.

sentences.t:
Orsilochus Remuli, quando ipsum horrebat adire,
hastam intorsit equo ferrumque sub aure reliquit.
sentences.l:
Orsilochus, of Remulus, since himself he shuddered to approach,
a spear hurled at the horse and the iron under the ear left.
sentences.i: Orsilochus, because he dreaded going against Remulus himself, hurled his spear at Remulus's horse and left the iron point lodged below its ear.
sentences.n: 'Remuli' depends on 'equo' in the next line, 'at the horse of Remulus', and is set early to contrast with 'ipsum', 'the man himself'. Orsilochus is on the Trojan side, Remulus a Latin. 'quando', 'since'. 'horrebat adire', 'shrank from approaching', with an infinitive. 'intorsit', 'hurled with a twist'. 'ferrum… reliquit', 'left the iron (in the wound)'. Elisions 'quand(o) ipsum', 'ipsu(m) horrebat', 'hast(am) intorsit'.

sentences.t:
Quo sonipes ictu furit arduus altaque iactat
vulneris impatiens arrecto pectore crura:
sentences.l:
At which blow the charger rages, rearing, and high flings,
of the wound impatient, with breast raised, its legs:
sentences.i: At the blow the charger went wild and reared, and, unable to bear the wound, flung its legs high with its chest lifted up:
sentences.n: 'Quo… ictu', connecting relative, 'at this blow'. 'sonipes', 'the charger', as at 600. 'arduus', 'steep, upright', rearing. 'alta… crura', 'high legs', framing the line, the forelegs thrown up. 'vulneris impatiens', 'not enduring the wound', the adjective with a genitive. 'vulneris' is printed with 'u' here, though Greenough elsewhere prints 'volnus'. 'arrecto pectore', ablative absolute. No elisions.

sentences.t: volvitur ille excussus humi.
sentences.l: rolls he, thrown off, on the ground.
sentences.i: its rider was thrown and rolled on the ground.
sentences.n: 'ille', Remulus, the rider, as against the horse. 'excussus', 'shaken off', as Aconteus was at 615. 'humi', locative, 'on the ground'. 'volvitur', passive in middle sense, 'rolls'. The brief sentence ends with a strong pause in the fourth foot. Elision 'ill(e) excussus'.

sentences.t:
Catillus Iollan
ingentemque animis, ingentem corpore et armis
deicit Herminium, nudo cui vertice fulva
caesaries nudique umeri, nec vulnera terrent:
sentences.l:
Catillus Iollas
and, huge in spirit, huge in body and arms,
brings down Herminius, on whose bare head tawny
hair and bare his shoulders, nor wounds frighten him:
sentences.i: Catillus brought down Iollas, and Herminius, mighty in spirit, mighty in body and arms, whose head was bare with its tawny hair, and his shoulders bare, and wounds did not frighten him:
sentences.n: Catillus, twin brother of Coras (Argive warriors from Tibur, VII.670–672), now kills two men; 'Cātillus' has a long first syllable, as VII.672 shows. 'Iollan', Greek accusative of 'Iollas', three syllables, I-ol-lan. 'ingentem animis, ingentem corpore', both of Herminius, the adjective repeated at the head of each phrase. 'deicit', 'casts down', present, three syllables, dē-i-cit. 'nudo cui vertice', 'to whom with bare head', 'cui', dative of possession, the verb supplied: 'he had tawny hair on his bare head, and bare shoulders'. 'caesaries', 'flowing hair'. Elisions 'ingentemqu(e) animis', 'corpor(e) et', 'nudiqu(e) umeri'.

sentences.t: tantus in arma patet.
sentences.l: so great, to arms he lies open.
sentences.i: so huge a target did he offer to the weapons.
sentences.n: 'tantus… patet', 'so great is he (as he) lies open', the size of the unarmoured man making him an easy mark. 'in arma', 'to arms', 'exposed to weapons'. The short sentence explains the last, with 'tantus' echoing 'ingentem… ingentem'. No elisions.

sentences.t:
Latos huic hasta per armos
acta tremit duplicatque virum transfixa dolore.
sentences.l:
Broad, for him, the spear through the shoulders
driven quivers, and doubles the man up, thrust through, with pain.
sentences.i: The spear driven through his broad shoulders quivered in the wound and, passing clean through, doubled him up with pain.
sentences.n: 'huic', dative of disadvantage, 'for him', 'his'. 'Latos… per armos', 'through the broad shoulders', framing 'huic hasta'; 'armi' are shoulders, a word used mostly of animals, and it plays against 'arma' just before. 'acta', 'driven'. 'tremit', 'quivers', in the wound. 'duplicat… virum', 'doubles the man up'. 'transfixa', perfect passive participle agreeing with 'hasta', 'driven right through' him. 'dolore', ablative of cause. No elisions.

sentences.t: Funditur ater ubique cruor;
sentences.l: Is poured, dark, everywhere the blood;
sentences.i: Dark blood flowed everywhere;
sentences.n: 'Funditur', 'is poured out', placed first. 'ater… cruor', 'dark blood', framing 'ubique'; 'cruor' is blood shed from a wound, as against 'sanguis', blood in the body. The battle widens from single kills to the whole field. No elisions.

sentences.t:
dant funera ferro
certantes pulchramque petunt per vulnera mortem.
sentences.l:
they give deaths with the sword,
striving, and a beautiful they seek through wounds death.
sentences.i: vying with each other, they dealt death with the sword and sought a glorious death through wounds.
sentences.n: 'dant funera', 'they give deaths', deal slaughter. 'ferro', 'with the sword', iron for the blade. 'certantes', 'competing', with each other in courage. 'pulchram… mortem', 'a beautiful death', framing 'petunt per vulnera': the 'fine death' in battle, the old heroic ideal. 'per vulnera', 'through wounds'. The part ends in the thick of the fight; Camilla's own exploits follow. No elisions.
